Queue::is, Queue::as¶

Back to Queue API Reference

Signature¶

template <class T>
bool is() const noexcept;

template <class T>
const T& as() const;

template <class T>
T& as();

What It Does¶

is<T>() and as<T>() are the template-based equivalents of is_series()/series() and their three siblings, for generic code written against a type parameter instead of a hardcoded accessor name – T is one of Series, Note, Timeline, or Duration. is<T>() checks whether the held payload is exactly T; as<T>() returns a reference to it.

The behavioral difference from the named accessors (series()/note()/timeline()/duration()) is in what happens on a kind mismatch: the named accessors throw a named failure naming both the method and the actual kind; as<T>() calls std::get<T> directly on the internal std::variant with no such check, so a mismatch throws a bare std::bad_variant_access instead, with no Queue-specific message.

Parameters¶

T (template parameter)

One of Series, Note, pluss::codeh::Timeline, or pluss::codeh::Duration.

Returns¶

is<T>() returns bool. as<T>() returns a reference to the payload, typed as T.

Errors¶

as<T>() throws std::bad_variant_access when T does not match the Queue’s actual kind(). Unlike the named accessors, the exception carries no message naming the actual kind – check is<T>() or kind() first if that information matters to the caller.

Examples¶

Example 1. is<T>() on a Note-holding Queue, true for the matching type and false for a mismatched one.

pluss::Queue q(pluss::make_note({"p", "q"}));
std::cout << "is<pluss::Note>(): " << q.is<pluss::Note>() << '\n';
std::cout << "is<pluss::Series>(): " << q.is<pluss::Series>() << '\n';
std::cout << "as<pluss::Note>().numel(): " << q.as<pluss::Note>().numel() << '\n';

Output¶

is<pluss::Note>(): true
is<pluss::Series>(): false
as<pluss::Note>().numel(): 2

Example 2. Calling as<T>() with the wrong T throws std::bad_variant_access, not a Queue-named message.

pluss::Queue q(pluss::make_note({"p", "q"}));
try {
  (void)q.as<pluss::Series>();
  std::cout << "as<pluss::Series>(): did not throw\n";
} catch (const std::bad_variant_access& e) {
  std::cout << "as<pluss::Series>() threw std::bad_variant_access: " << e.what() << '\n';
}

Output¶

as<pluss::Series>() threw std::bad_variant_access: bad_variant_access

std::bad_variant_access::what() gives the generic library message "bad_variant_access", with no mention of Queue, Series, or Note – check is<T>() first (as in Example 1) when the caller needs to know why the access would fail, rather than catching the exception to find out.

See Also¶

  • accessors: the named, non-templated equivalents, which throw a more informative message on a kind mismatch.

  • kind: is_series()/is_note()/is_timeline()/ is_duration(), the non-templated equivalent of is<T>().
